blocks.text: JavaScript JSON Values
JSON Value Types
In JSON, values must be one of the following data types:
JSON Objects
A JSON object is enclosed in curly braces { }.
A JSON object contains one or more properties.

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Properties comes in name/value pairs.
Names must be strings enclosed in double quotes.
Values can be any valid JSON value:

rows: A sequence of characters enclosed in double quotes
The literal values true or false
The literal value null to indicate the absence of a value
An list of values enclosed in square brackets
A collection of key/value pairs enclosed in curly braces

blocks.text: Property values can be objects.

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Property values can be arrays:

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: JSON Arrays
A JSON array is enclosed in square brackets [ ].
An array contains an ordered list of values.

[

  "Ford",

  "Volvo",

  "BMW"

]
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Array values can be any valid JSON value.

rows: A sequence of characters enclosed in double quotes
The literal values true or false
The literal value null to indicate the absence of a value
An list of values enclosed in square brackets
A collection of key/value pairs enclosed in curly braces

blocks.text: Nested Values
Objects and arrays can contain other objects and arrays.

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Nested objects and arrays make it possible to represent complex data structures.
JSON String values
A JSON string value is a sequence of zero or more Unicode characters enclosed in double quotes.

""

"Hello World!"

"He said, \"Hello!\""

"\u00A9 2026"
blocks.caption: Examples
Examples

blocks.text: JSON strings represent special characters using a backslash (\) escape syntax:
To be valid, JSON strings require double quotes (unlike JavaScript, which permits single quotes).
JSON Number Values
JSON number values can be integers or floating-point numbers.

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text:
JSON does not distinguish between different numeric types.
It treats integers and floating-point decimals under a single "number" category.

rows:
Numbers containing a decimal point
followed by at least one digit
Numbers using e/E to indicate power of 10

blocks.text: JSON numbers requires absolute structural precision.
Many formats allowed in standard programming languages will break a JSON parser:

rows: "42" turns the value into a JSON string.
Integers can not be padded with zeros (05).
Hexadecimal and Octal formats are invalid (0x7A).

blocks.text: JSON Boolean Values
JSON supports the Boolean values true and false.

blocks.caption: Example

rows: "true" turns the value into a JSON string.
Variations like TRUE, FALSE, True, or False are invalid.
JSON does not accept numbers like 1 or 0 as boolean replacements.

blocks.text: JSON Null
The value null represents an empty value.

blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: undefined Is Not a JSON Value
JSON supports null, but not undefined.

blocks.text: Unsupported JavaScript Values
JSON has a small, strict syntax.
These JavaScript values cannot be represented in JSON:
These values must be converted before they can be stored as JSON.
Date Values
Date objects are not allowed in JSON.
If you need to include a date, write it as a string.
You can convert it back into a date object later:
const text = '{"name":"John", "birth":"1986-12-14"}';
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Functions as Values

blocks.caption: Wrong

blocks.text: If you need to save a function, save it as a string.
You can convert it back into a function later.
const text = '{"name":"John", "age":"function () {return 30;}';
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: Convertion Values
You will learn more about converting JavaScript values in the next chapters.
Both JSON.parse() and JSON.stringify() have options to convert values between formats.
